share_verdict: Bombay, not antiquity. Restore the components, not the myth.

ingredients.name: tomato
ingredients.function: acid and colour. Also a Columbian-exchange arrival

ingredients.name: cauliflower and capsicum
ingredients.function: bulk. Both are post-classical arrivals in Indian cooking

ingredients.name: pav (refined-flour bread roll)
ingredients.function: the vehicle. Yeast-leavened refined-flour bread, Portuguese in origin

ingredients.name: butter
ingredients.function: the finish, and most of what people are actually eating it for

method_reconstructed: Boil and mash potato and mixed vegetables.
Fry onion, tomato and spice blend in butter; fold the mash through.
Split and griddle the pav in butter.
contested_points: Almost every defining ingredient here arrived after the classical texts. This is a 19th-century Bombay dish and reads as one.
Its usual origin story ties it to mill-worker meals in Bombay; the details of that account vary between tellings.

changed.driver: there is no ancestor to recover; the parts can still be improved on their own terms

ingredients: 2 cups cooked white peas or kabuli chana, half of it mashed, carrying part of the load the potato usually carries alone
Pav made with coarse whole wheat, or a millet flatbread if you would rather skip the roll
3 tbsp cold-pressed groundnut oil, plus a little ghee to finish
Ginger, garlic, black pepper, your usual spice blend
steps: Cook the peas or chana until soft. Mash half, leave half whole.
Fry ginger, garlic and the spice blend in the oil; add tomato and cook down properly, this is the step street vendors do not rush and home cooks do.
Fold in the vegetables and the pulse, mash to the texture you want, simmer ten minutes.
Griddle the bread in a little ghee.
Swapping part of the potato for a pulse moves protein and fibre up and glycaemic load down, without changing what the dish is. The frying fat is doing real flavour work here, so it is worth naming.

verification.note: Classed MODERN_DISH. No ancient original is claimed and no locus is cited, so there is no citation to verify.
